cultivar: Taiwanese cultivars (No. 12 Jin Xuan, No. 17) on the oolong farms; assamica-type bushes on older plantations; some Japanese cultivars on farms making steamed tea
processing: Two styles: a Chinese-style pan-fired tea, rolled and dried after wok or drum firing, and a Japanese-style steamed, needle-rolled tea made on a few farms for the domestic café trade; both are unshaded and fully green.
harvest_season: Picked through the year on the northern hills; the cool dry season from November to February and the early hot-season pick in March give the sweetest, cleanest green tea.
appearance_dry: Pan-fired lots: curled dark green leaves with some tips; steamed lots: flat dark green needles. Both smell fresh and faintly toasty.
appearance_liquor: Pale yellow-green and clear (steamed lots slightly cloudy).
appearance_wet: Opened mid-sized green leaves, uniform on the cultivar farms.
taste_profile: Mild and clean: fresh greens and a light toastiness in the pan-fired style, grassier and brothier in the steamed style, with gentle sweetness, low bitterness and a short finish.

brewing.notes: Cooled water and a short first steep; the Thai habit of brewing green tea with boiling water in a glass is what gives it a reputation for bitterness it does not deserve. Good iced with a squeeze of lime.

vintage_note: Sold as the current year's lot, usually vacuum-packed in 100–200 g foil without a harvest date, by farm or brand; the cool-season harvest is the one to ask for. It is a fresh green tea, best within a year, and most of it is drunk at home in Thailand or goes into the green-tea-latte and bottled-tea trade.
description:
Green tea is a sideline in Thailand's northern tea country, which built its reputation on oolong, but the same farms around Mae Salong, Mae Chan and the Doi Tung royal project also fire some of their leaf green, and the result is a pleasant, mild tea that deserves to be better known than the bottled, sweetened 'green tea' that dominates Thai supermarket shelves.

Most of it is pan-fired in the Chinese manner from the Taiwanese cultivars the farms grow for oolong, which gives a soft, slightly toasty tea with a buttery hint from the Jin Xuan bushes. A few producers are reported to make Japanese-style steamed green tea for cafés serving green tea lattes and for the domestic health-tea market, with flat needle leaves and a grassier, brothier cup. Neither is shaded, and neither is trying to be delicate; they are everyday greens from a warm climate.

In the cup, expect fresh greens, mild sweetness and low bitterness, with the pan-fired version nuttier and the steamed version more like a plain bancha or an everyday sencha. Brewed with cooled water it is easy and clean; brewed the way it is often served in Thailand, with boiling water in a glass, it turns bitter quickly. It takes well to ice and to lime.

It is sold vacuum-packed by farm, often without a harvest date, and the cool-season lots are the ones worth buying; rainy-season leaf is flat. 'Thai green tea' on a bottle or a sachet is usually a sweetened, flavoured drink and tells you nothing about the leaf. Buy from a named farm, and treat it as a fresh tea to finish within the year.

If you want the best of the Thai hills, their oolongs No. 12 and No. 17 are the stronger suit; the green tea is a good hot-weather pot and a pleasant base for a homemade Thai green tea latte.
sources_note: Thai green tea is a small, loosely defined product and this card generalises across several Chiang Rai farms; the existence of Japanese-style steamed lots is based on farm offerings seen in the trade. The umbrella article chosen is the Mae Salong village article rather than a tea article, since no Thai green tea article exists.
history: Green tea from Chiang Rai is a sideline of the northern hill farms, which are better known for oolong. Little is documented about it as a distinct tea: it has no fixed style or standard, and farms simply make some of their leaf green. Treat it as a loose description of an everyday product rather than a named traditional tea.
